ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, an ideal transformer has a turns ratio of the primary and secondary coils of 4:1. The primary coil is connected in series with a variable resistor and then connected to a sinusoidal AC power supply; in the secondary coil circuit, the resistance of the fixed resistor is R0, the resistance of the load resistor is R=11R0, and it is an ideal voltmeter. Now the resistance of the load resistor is reduced to R=5R0, while keeping the transformer input current unchanged. At this time the voltmeter reading is 5.0V, then (　　)
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: The original effective value of the voltage across the primary coil is about 48V

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, an ideal transformer has a turns ratio of the primary and secondary coils of 4:1. The primary coil is connected in series with a variable resistor and then connected to a sinusoidal AC power supply; in the secondary coil circuit, the resistance of the fixed resistor is R0, and the original load resistor is R=11R0. Now the load resistance is reduced to R=5R0, while keeping the transformer input current unchanged. At this time the voltmeter reading is 5.0V. Find about how many V the original effective value of the voltage across the primary coil is.
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: The original effective value of the voltage across the primary coil is about 48V
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: on the left of the figure is a sinusoidal AC power supply, and the primary coil is connected in series with a variable resistor and then connected to the power supply; in the middle is an ideal transformer. In the secondary coil circuit on the right, the upper end of the secondary coil passes through the fixed resistor R0 and then reaches the upper node; the load resistor R on the right is connected between this upper node and the lower common node, and the ideal voltmeter V is also connected between the same upper node and the lower common node, so the voltmeter measures the voltage across the load resistor R. Then reason: let the secondary coil current be I. After the load is reduced, R=5R0, and the voltmeter reading is 5.0V. The ideal voltmeter does not shunt current, so the load current equals the secondary coil current, I·5R0=5.0V, giving I R0=1.0V. Keeping the transformer input current unchanged, and with the turns ratio of the ideal transformer unchanged, the secondary coil current I is also unchanged. Originally when R=11R0, the voltage across the secondary coil was U2=I(R0+11R0)=12IR0=12V. The turns ratio of the primary and secondary coils is 4:1, so the original effective value of the voltage across the primary coil is U1=4U2=4×12V=48V. Final answer: about 48V.
